title: Patience Until the Lord Comes, and the Prayer of Faith
summary: James pronounces judgment on rich landowners who hoarded wealth, withheld wages, and condemned the innocent. He urges suffering believers to be patient like a farmer waiting for rain, like the prophets, and like Job, because the Lord's coming is near. He forbids oaths, calls for prayer in every circumstance, including prayer and anointing by the elders for the sick, and ends by urging believers to bring back anyone who wanders from the truth.
story: Chapter 4 ended by rebuking merchants who planned their future without God. Chapter 5 turns to the landowning rich with even sharper words, in the style of the Old Testament prophets, and then to the poor believers who suffer under them. The letter began with trials and perseverance (1:2-4), and it now returns to that theme, setting endurance in the light of the Lord's coming. The last verses gather the community around prayer, confession, and care for the sick and the straying, so that the letter ends not with a formal farewell but with a picture of a church that holds its members fast.
historical:
The oppression James describes was real in the economy of Roman Palestine and much of the empire. Large estates were worked by hired day laborers, who depended on being paid each evening to feed their families. The law of Moses required prompt payment (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15), and the prophets condemned landowners who defrauded workers (Jeremiah 22:13; Malachi 3:5). James's words that the laborers' cries “have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts” echo Isaiah 5:9 and use the ancient title for God as commander of heaven's armies (in Greek, Sabaoth). The charge that the rich condemned and murdered the righteous may refer to the poor ruined through the courts, or to specific killings.

The fall and spring rains (sometimes called the early and late rains) are a feature of the climate of Palestine and Syria: rain in autumn, around October and November, softens the ground for planting, and rain in spring, around March and April, fills out the grain before harvest (Deuteronomy 11:14). A farmer could do nothing to hurry them.
cultural:
Wealth in the ancient world was often stored as fine clothing, gold and silver, and grain. Clothes could be eaten by moths, and metals could tarnish, and James's picture of rotting riches recalls Jesus' warning about treasures on earth (Matthew 6:19-20). Oaths were used constantly in ancient speech to guarantee truthfulness, sometimes by heaven or earth to avoid using God's name directly, and Jesus had forbidden this evasive practice (Matthew 5:33-37), which James echoes nearly word for word.

Olive oil was used in the ancient world as medicine, applied to wounds and ailments (compare Luke 10:34), and also for anointing in religious settings, marking a person or object as set apart for God. Jesus' disciples anointed the sick with oil and healed them (Mark 6:13). The elders were the recognized leaders of the congregation, a pattern taken over from the synagogue. James's instruction brings the sick person into the care of the whole church and into the presence of God through prayer.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-6 are a prophetic oracle of judgment, introduced by “Come now” as in 4:13, full of vivid images (rotted riches, moth-eaten clothes, corroded gold, crying wages, fattened hearts). James does not seem to expect the rich to read it; like the prophets' oracles against the nations, it is spoken over the oppressors for the sake of the oppressed. Verses 7-11 turn to the believers with three examples of patience (the farmer, the prophets, Job) and three reminders of the Lord's nearness. Verses 12-20 form a closing section: “Above all” introduces the command against oaths, then a series of situations (suffering, cheerfulness, sickness, sin) each answered with prayer or praise, the example of Elijah, and a final word about restoring the wanderer.

outline.t: The prayer of faith for the suffering and the sick
Bringing back the one who wanders

doctrines.note: God hears the cries of the defrauded, and injustice will be judged. “The Judge is standing at the door”, both for the oppressive rich and for believers tempted to grumble against one another.
Patience is grounded in the promise that “the Lord’s coming is near.” Christian hope does not deny present suffering; it waits with the confidence of a farmer who knows the rains will come.

Prayer is the right response to every condition of life: suffering, joy, sickness, and sin. “The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail”, and Elijah shows that such a person is “a man just like us.”

James offers Job and the prophets as examples of endurance, and reminds readers that “The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.” The outcome of Job's story shows that suffering does not have the last word.

words.note: Makrothumeō, to be patient or long-suffering, literally to be long-tempered. It describes the ability to bear with people and circumstances without retaliation or despair. James uses it three times in verses 7-8, and the related noun in verse 10. In the Greek Old Testament the same word family describes God's own slowness to anger.

Parousia, coming, presence, or arrival. In the Greek world it could describe the official visit of a ruler to a city. The New Testament uses it for the return of Christ in glory (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:15). James says this coming is near, a nearness that shapes behavior now.

Aleiphō, to anoint, often with oil. It is the ordinary word for rubbing or applying oil, used for medical care, grooming, and honoring guests, and it differs from chriō, the word used for sacred anointing of kings and of Christ. Interpreters debate whether James's anointing is primarily medical, symbolic, or sacramental.

Presbuteros, elder. The word means an older man, and it became the title for leaders of synagogues and then of Christian congregations (Acts 14:23; 1 Peter 5:1). James assumes that each church has elders and that their care includes praying for the sick.

christ: Christ appears in this chapter as the coming Lord and Judge. James twice speaks of “the Lord’s coming”, and he pictures the Judge standing at the door, an image Jesus used of the nearness of the Son of Man (Mark 13:29). The command against oaths repeats Jesus' teaching almost exactly. The call to anoint the sick “in the name of the Lord” and the promise that “The Lord will raise him up” recall Jesus' ministry of healing and the work of his disciples in his name (Mark 6:13; Acts 3:6). The final verses about turning a sinner back reflect Jesus' parables of the lost sheep and the lost son (Luke 15), and the promise to cover a multitude of sins points to the forgiveness he secured.

hard.q: Does James promise that anyone who is prayed for with faith will be physically healed?
hard.a:
James says that “the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick” and that the Lord will raise him up. Christians read this in several ways. Many take it as a real promise of God's help, which often comes as physical healing but is ultimately fulfilled in the resurrection, when God will raise his people fully; the Greek words for restore and raise up (the verb sōzō, to save, and egeirō, to raise) can carry both meanings. Others emphasize that the promise depends on God's will, as Paul's own unhealed thorn in the flesh shows (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches see in these verses the basis of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick. Many Protestants see the oil as medicinal, symbolic, or both, and some churches practice anointing with prayer as James describes. None of these readings sets prayer against medical care; oil itself was a medicine in James's day.

What the passage does not teach is that illness that persists is a sign of weak faith or hidden sin. James says only “If he has sinned”, not that sickness always comes from sin. Anyone who is sick, in pain, or in despair should call on both the church and qualified medical help, and anyone thinking of harming themselves should reach out immediately to a trusted person or to emergency services.

questions: James addresses the rich in the language of the prophets. Where does our economic life, including what we buy and whom we pay, fall under his warning?
What helps you to wait patiently, like the farmer, when relief does not come quickly?
Verses 13-20 picture a church that prays, confesses, and pursues those who wander. What would it take for your community to practice this more fully?
